text.title: KPI Drift Alarm Template Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules with rationale + source for kpi-drift-alarm-template. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Each KPI MUST have a rolling baseline of at least 4 cycles; baselines shorter than 4 cycles are auto-rejected as noisy.
rule.rationale: With one or two cycles there is no estimate of the KPI's normal variation, so every ordinary fluctuation registers as drift and the channel fills with noise until readers stop opening it. Four cycles is roughly where a deviation can be judged against the metric's own spread rather than against a single previous number. The window rolls because the level itself moves, and a frozen baseline turns legitimate growth into a permanent alarm.

rule.statement: Deviation threshold MUST specify direction (above / below / either); thresholds without direction are forbidden because drift can be benign or malignant per direction.
rule.rationale: Most KPIs are asymmetric in meaning: conversion falling is a problem, conversion rising is not, and a direction-blind threshold announces the good news with the same urgency as the bad. Within a few cycles readers learn that half the alarms are congratulations and stop distinguishing. Stating the direction also forces the author to record what the metric is supposed to mean, which is the assumption that otherwise lives only in someone's head.

rule.statement: Alarms MUST be two-class: warning (1 sigma deviation) + critical (2 sigma deviation); single-class alarms produce alarm fatigue.
rule.rationale: A single class forces one threshold to serve two incompatible jobs, so it ends up either tight enough to flood the channel with things nobody acts on, or loose enough that the first signal arrives after the damage is done. Splitting the tiers lets the sensitive one carry information and the severe one carry obligation, so the reader can tell without investigating which alarms demand a response today.

rule.statement: After firing, an alarm is suppressed for a defined window (default 1 cycle) to avoid storm; suppression window MUST be configured per KPI.
rule.rationale: A drifted KPI stays drifted until someone fixes it, so an unsuppressed alarm re-announces the same known condition every cycle and buries genuinely new alarms in the repetition. The window is per KPI because the right amount of silence depends on the metric's cadence and on how fast a fix could plausibly land; one global setting either muzzles a fast-moving metric or lets a slow one nag through a whole quarter.

rule.statement: If the same alarm fires for 3 consecutive cycles, escalation routes it to a named owner; silent re-firing is forbidden.
rule.rationale: Suppression buys quiet, and quiet is exactly how an unowned problem survives: the alarm keeps re-firing into a channel where everyone assumes someone else has it, while the drift compounds. Counting consecutive fires turns persistence itself into the trigger, and routing to a named person rather than a channel is what makes the next step somebody's job instead of the group's.

rule.statement: Every alarm message MUST include a deep link to the underlying chart / query; alarms without data context are forbidden.
rule.rationale: An alarm that states only a number makes the reader reconstruct the query before they can tell a real shift from a broken data pipeline, and that cost is paid at the moment they have least time, so the alarm is deferred and then forgotten. The link is also the cheapest way to recognise a false positive; without it, spurious and genuine alarms are indistinguishable on arrival and the whole channel loses credibility at the same rate.

rule.statement: Every fired alarm MUST be closed with a written resolution (root cause, action taken); open alarms older than 1 cycle escalate.
rule.rationale: Without a written close, a recurrence next quarter is investigated from scratch by whoever is on duty, and a diagnosis the engagement already paid for is re-derived. The log is also the only way to distinguish an alarm that was resolved from one that was silently tolerated, since both look identical from outside. Escalating alarms left open past a cycle exists because "still open" is where alarms go to be forgotten, not a state anyone deliberately chooses.

rule.statement: If KPI history is shorter than 4 cycles or no on-call coverage exists, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: Below four cycles the baseline is a guess dressed as a threshold, and the alarms it emits carry an authority the underlying data does not support. Absent on-call coverage is worse than having no alarm at all: the alarms fire into an empty room, the team learns that this channel can be ignored, and that habit carries straight over to the alarms that eventually do matter.
